value.text: Another round of heavy rain in Florida is once again raising concerns about flooding and flood insurance. According to the Insurance Information Institute, as much as 80% of Florida homeowners don't carry flood insurance, even though just one inch of water in a home can cause $25,000 in damage.WATCH REPORT BELOW: "Everyone is in a flood zone," says Lee Wiglesworth of Wiglesworth Rindom Insurance in Stuart. "It's just a matter of if you're in a high risk or a low risk." He said many pass on the coverage because of costs, being in a low-risk zone and also not fully understanding their homeowners policy. "If a hurricane comes and creates a flooding event, they think I have hurricane coverage," he said. But those claims are often denied since homeowners policies only cover wind damage. Experts say relying on FEMA in flood situations can leave homeowners short, since FEMA grants will cover temporary housing and essential repairs. National flood insurance will cover $250,000 on the structure and $100,000 on the contents of a home. Costs for flood insurance can vary from $600 to $1,300 a year. In addition to national flood insurance, there are also options for flood insurance with private insurers, and there are waiting periods before policies become active.

Heavy rain moved across the area Wednesday, flooding roads in parts of West Palm Beach. The soggy weather created a messy drive as people prepared to travel for Thanksgiving.Several areas of downtown West Palm Beach saw significant standing water as rain continued to fall.WATCH REPORT BELOW: At South Flagler Drive and Barcelona Road, water covered the roadway, forcing some drivers to turn around rather than attempt to make it through.WPTV reporter Christy Waite saw several cars turn around to avoid the area.Flooding was visible across several parts of the city. Near Ann Norton Sculpture Gardens, Palm Beach Atlantic University and the Palm Beach County Yacht Club, streets filled with water and even traffic cones could be seen floating in the roadway.Across from Elisabetta's Ristorante in downtown West Palm Beach, the water rose past Waite's boot as vehicles, including buses, continued navigating the flooded streets.From downtown, Waite traveled north to Lone Pine Estates in Riviera Beach, a neighborhood that has been hit especially hard by flooding this month.Neighbor Lacey Stone previously described how quickly conditions deteriorated."I have lived in Florida my whole life, and I have never seen anything like this; it just got worse and worse," Stone said.The water in the neighborhood has since receded, but signs of the earlier flooding remain.Some residents still have sandbags outside their homes, while others continue dealing with damage left behind. Residents like Stephanie Gabriel never want to experience something like this again. "This has been a devastating experience, and seeing all the damage it has caused is heart-wrenching," Gabriel said.The flooding wasn't limited to the areas WPTV visited.As Waite headed back to the station, she found even more standing water, this time in WPTV’s own parking lot in West Palm Beach.

Thanksgiving travelers at President Donald J. Trump International Airport were navigating dozens of delayed flights Wednesday, but WPTV observed no cancellations during its reporting as millions of Americans took to the skies ahead of the holiday.WATCH BELOW: Thanksgiving travelers navigate delaysThe Transportation Security Administration (TSA) expects to screen about 17.6 million passengers nationwide between Tuesday and Monday, with more than 3 million passengers expected Sunday, the busiest day of the Thanksgiving travel period.Nationwide, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is forecasting more than 417,000 flights during the nine-day Thanksgiving travel period. The federal agency has also warned that weather could affect flights as storms move across several parts of the country. Across South Florida, conditions varied Wednesday. Travelers reported long security lines at Miami International Airport and Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport, while FlightAware recorded more than 1,100 delays nationwide Wednesday morning.Despite delays, many travelers WPTV met in Palm Beach County were focused less on the wait and more on who was waiting for them at the end of the trip.Yvonne Jackson arrived from Toronto to spend Thanksgiving with family."The end result is we're here, we're happy, and we can't wait to be with the family tomorrow," Jackson said.Her flight took longer than expected as weather complicated the final approach."The pilot said they had to circle because the ground was too wet, so we were up there in the clouds and just felt a bit nervous," Jackson said.Eventually, the flight made it to the ground."Finally, he landed with a thud, and we all clapped," she said.On the other side of the arrival doors, Debbie Hunter was waiting for a reunion of her own."I'm here to pick up my son," Hunter said. "He's flying in from Washington, D.C. for Thanksgiving."Her son recently turned 32, making the homecoming a celebration of both his birthday and the holiday."Extremely excited," Hunter said. "I love to have my young man come home."While some families were welcoming relatives home, Barbara Cook and Brian Cook were preparing to fly out to see theirs."We were expecting the worst," they said. "So far, it hasn't been too bad."Their flight to New York's LaGuardia Airport was delayed, meaning their reunion with their daughter and her family would have to wait."Probably won't see our family till tomorrow," they said.But there is an especially important reason to make the trip."She has a newborn and a 2-year-old," Barbara Cook said. "So we're excited to see our 10th grandchild."Brian Cook summed up the motivation behind the holiday journey."It's all about family," he said.The TSA recommends arriving at least two hours before a domestic flight and three hours before an international flight during the busy Thanksgiving travel period.TSA says passengers should also allow extra time for parking, airline check-in, checking bags and security screening. Travelers should check directly with their airline for the latest flight information before leaving for the airport. The FAA is also encouraging passengers to plan ahead because weather could affect flights throughout the holiday week. For many travelers making their way through Palm Beach County on Wednesday, however, the delays were easier to accept knowing family was waiting at the other end.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

A water meter data collection issue in Martin County caused some utility customers to receive unusually high water bills, according to Martin County Utilities.The county said the problem dates back about five months and affected the reporting of water usage for some customers.WATCH REPORT BELOW: After the issue was corrected, water usage that had not previously been reported was reflected on a single month's bill, resulting in a higher-than-normal charge for affected customers.Martin County Utilities said the issue affects some customers in these communities:Legacy CoveHighlands ReserveCove IsleMontego CoveEmerald LakesSavannah OaksCove LakesRiver MarinaRiver Marina EstatesRocky PointCustomers with questions about their bills or who need assistance can contact Martin County Utilities customer service at cservice@martin.fl.us. The county said a customer service representative can work with affected residents to establish a payment arrangement.Martin County Utilities said it has since implemented additional training and safeguards within its data collection software.Have you been affected? Let us know on our Facebook page!

Millions of people are hitting the road this Thanksgiving holiday, but getting to their final destination isn't always going according to plan.Heavy rain moved across South Florida on Wednesday, adding another challenge for drivers traveling to spend the holiday with family and friends.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE HERE: Even with rain in the forecast, some travelers weren't prepared for the unexpected delays they encountered along the way.More than 4.2 million Floridians are expected to travel by car for Thanksgiving, according to AAA. Nationwide, the Federal Aviation Administration also expects more than 417,000 flights during the nine-day Thanksgiving travel period, making it the busiest Thanksgiving travel stretch in 16 years.For many travelers, the goal was simply getting home."I haven't been home in like a month and a half," one traveler said.Others were making their way to South Florida, including one man who said, "We're trying to get to Miami."But the journey became more complicated for drivers on Florida's Turnpike in Palm Beach County.A jackknifed tractor-trailer shut down the southbound lanes, leaving drivers stuck in standstill traffic. The delay was an unexpected hurdle for people already navigating wet roads and holiday congestion.One man making the trip from Georgia to Miami was among those caught in the backup. Another traveler said a drive that typically takes two hours had quickly turned into three."We knew it was going to rain today all day long," one driver said.Another woman said she expected some delays because of the weather but was surprised by how long traffic had come to a stop."Well, we didn't expect to be sitting here an hour for sure. We expected some delays because of rain and potential flooding," she said.The delay was so significant that she was considering changing her plans altogether."We actually might, because it's been so long, might turn around and go back to my daughter's house, in West Palm Beach," she said.Others found ways to make the unexpected wait a little more entertaining. One child said the family was passing the time by playing a game."We're playing like a Heads Up game," the child said.For another traveler, the immediate priority was getting traffic moving again — and finding a bathroom."So we're just hoping this gets moving soon so we can find a Jiffy John somewhere," the traveler said.Despite the rain and unexpected traffic backups, travelers shared one common goal: making it to their loved ones in time for Thanksgiving.For drivers still making the trip, officials recommend allowing extra travel time, slowing down on wet roads and staying alert for changing traffic conditions.

New police body-camera video shows officers taking a man into custody after a 19-year-old woman reported being attacked along Boca Raton’s El Rio Trail. Now, people who frequent the trail say the attack, along with an earlier incident involving the same suspect at the same location, is making them reconsider their safety and call for a greater police presence.WATCH: El Rio Trail assault arrest caught on bodycam amid safety concernsBodycam shows suspect being taken into custodyPolice body-camera video shows officers taking 36-year-old LaPaul Jackson of Miami Gardens into custody following Monday’s attack.According to a Boca Raton police report, the 19-year-old woman was walking along El Rio Trail around 11:30 a.m. when Jackson allegedly approached her from behind with a knife and forced her into a wooded area.Police said the woman was attacked before she managed to escape and return to the trail, where someone helped her call 911. Investigators said she suffered multiple cuts.Police used the location of the woman’s stolen cellphone to track Jackson to a Palm Tran bus, according to the police affidavit.Jackson faces seven charges, including kidnapping, sexual battery with a deadly weapon, robbery with a weapon and tampering with a victim. Police records also show he is accused of violating his pretrial release in connection with an August robbery case.Attack raises safety concerns along El Rio TrailPeople who regularly walk and exercise along El Rio Trail told WPTV the daytime attack has changed how they think about their safety.“In shock, especially because it happened so early in the morning,” Isabel Chambers told WPTV.Luiz Souza said he was disappointed and believes more attention needs to be paid to the area.“Disappointment because the police is supposed to take care a little better of this place,” Souza said.Another person said the attack will make her reconsider walking the trail by herself.“Well, I’m going to think twice now about going alone,” she said.Previous incident adds to concernsThe concerns come as WPTV learned Jackson had previously been arrested in connection with another incident at the same location on El Rio Trail.According to police records, Jackson allegedly pushed a woman to the ground and stole her cellphone during an Aug. 1 incident. The affidavit says Jackson was on pretrial release in that case when the November incident occurred.Marvin Montoya told WPTV in Spanish that learning about the incidents caught him by surprise.“It surprises me, and I feel bad because if he hurt a woman or a young girl, he could hurt anyone,” Montoya said.Montoya added that he was glad Jackson was in custody.Calls for more police presenceWPTV asked Boca Raton police about the wooded encampment near the trail where investigators said Monday’s attack continued.Police said the property is privately owned, which presents an enforcement challenge because officers cannot enter simply to issue trespass warnings. Police confirmed previous arrests have been made in the area.Following the two incidents, people WPTV spoke with said they would like to see a more visible police presence along El Rio Trail.“It’d be nice to know that there’s somebody keeping an eye out for people,” one person said.More details from police recordsThe police affidavit provides additional details about how investigators tracked down Jackson.Police said the woman’s stolen iPhone had Life360 enabled, allowing her mother to provide officers with live location information. Investigators followed the phone’s movement to a Palm Tran bus near Northeast 20th Street and North Federal Highway.Officers found Jackson on the bus, according to the affidavit. Police also reported recovering the woman’s cellphone from the rear of the bus.Investigators said they recovered a large green serrated knife near El Rio Trail that the woman identified as the weapon used during the attack.According to the affidavit, officers also found a backpack in Jackson’s possession containing items including zip ties, duct tape, masks and a dark-colored long-sleeve jacket.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Federal disaster aid is now available for residents in Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast affected by recent flooding.FEMA announced late Tuesday that federal disaster assistance is available to individuals and families in Indian River, Martin, Okeechobee, Palm Beach, St. Lucie and Brevard counties as recovery efforts continue.U.S. Rep. Lois Frankel said in a statement the declaration unlocks critical federal recovery resources for residents, businesses and local governments devastated by the flooding.The assistance can include grants for temporary housing and home repairs, low-cost loans to cover uninsured property losses and other programs designed to help people recover from the disaster.Residents who suffered damage or other losses should first file a claim with their insurance provider. They can then apply for FEMA assistance through DisasterAssistance.gov, by calling 1-800-621-3362 or through the FEMA App.Those who use a relay service, including video relay or captioned telephone services, should provide FEMA with the number for that service when applying.Federal funding is also available on a cost-sharing basis to state, tribal and eligible local governments, as well as certain private nonprofit organizations, for debris removal and emergency protective measures. That assistance is available in Palm Beach, Martin, Indian River, Okeechobee, Brevard and Hardee, counties.Frankel said that Palm Beach County officials estimate that $53 million in disaster assistance is needed countywide — nearly $35 million to help individuals and families recover and more than $18 million to help local governments cover emergency response and cleanup costs.Additional counties could be designated for federal assistance later, depending on the results of continuing damage assessments.What residents should do:File a claim with their insurance provider.Apply for federal assistance at DisasterAssistance.gov, through the FEMA App or by calling 1-800-621-3362.Severe storms and flooding have impacted parts of Florida since Oct. 31, prompting the state to ask for the federal disaster declaration.

In Fort Pierce, behind the doors of A Future Worth Fighting 4, they embody what the City stands for.“Here, this community is a big fighting community. If you’re from Fort Pierce, you know how we get down," owner Darrion Henry said.How they get down at A Future Worth Fighting 4 was on full display at the 2026 Florida State Police Athletic League.WATCH: A local boxing gym brings the two C's: community and championshipsThey finished with three state champions, a silver medalist, and a second-place overall team finish, and the star of the Tournament was none other than Justice Henry. He credits the gym's family-like atmosphere and tough-love environment for his success.“This gym has been the biggest part of my life. I’ve been boxing since I was eight years old, and this became a home for our own little community and us, with everyone we bring in here,” said Henry.While Henry has been boxing since he was eight, he has a teammate, Frantzner Jean, who’s just getting started but is already making a name for himself after winning his first fight by unanimous decision.“It felt pretty fun; I just like the dopamine rush from it,” said Jean.Every day after school, kids fill the gym to learn the sweet science of boxing, but there's one rule: you have to go to school every day.“I’m a teacher at Dan McCarty, so I can see how their behavior has changed, and now I have a lot of kids who show up to school because they know if they don’t show up to school, I’m going to get on them,” said Henry.One of the kids taking the school-first approach is Michael Sanchez, whose dad signed him up for classes, but now he’s ready to take this sport as far as it can go.“I ended up liking it because I can learn from it, like discipline and hard work,” said Sanchez.

With Thanksgiving approaching, West Palm Beach police officers are helping make sure local families and individuals have a meal for the holiday.THE FUND, a nonprofit that supports the West Palm Beach Police Department, provided 150 Thanksgiving meals for officers to deliver to residents in need across the city.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Officers loaded the meals into police vehicles Tuesday morning at Heart and Soul Park on North Rosemary Avenue before taking them directly to residents' homes.According to organizers, police officers identified the families and individuals who could use additional support during the holiday season.The effort is a collaboration between THE FUND and the West Palm Beach Police Department.THE FUND is a nonprofit organization that works to supplement resources for the police department beyond what is available through the city's budget. The organization says its broader mission is to support officers while helping improve public safety and quality of life in West Palm Beach.

An attorney for the developer behind the controversial Project Tango data center warned Palm Beach County of "significant and potentially catastrophic financial liability" if an expansion wasn't approved, according to a 180-page letter obtained by WPTV's Michael Hoffman. Ten days after the letter was sent, Palm Beach County zoning staff approved the expansion.The letter represents a new development in WPTV's nearly yearlong coverage of Project Tango and raises new questions about the October decision that allowed the project to triple its data center space without another vote by county commissioners.In July, Palm Beach County commissioners denied a separate proposal to expand the project. Then in October, county staff administratively approved another expansion.The letter from Project Tango attorney Ethan Loeb was sent before that October approval and threatened significant legal action if county staff did not approve the expansion.The 180-page letter included legal threats against Palm Beach County and a personal threat of legal action against county Zoning Director Wendy Hernandez.According to the letter, denying the expansion could result in "significant and potentially catastrophic financial liability."The letter went further, contending potential damages involving PBA Holdings could be "so significant that it would be impossible for the county to financially sustain the damages that PBA Holdings would recover."Ten days later, zoning staff approved the expansion.Hoffman spoke with District 6 Commissioner Katherine Waldron, who represents the area where the project would be located.Waldron said she believes the letter's threat against a county employee calls the approval process into question."That letter comes out threatening not just the county, but to one of our zoning people, and I think that that corrupts the process, and we should consider overturning the decision because of that," Waldron said.Among the issues raised in the letter were additional requirements placed on Project Tango, including continuous sound studies and real-time public noise monitoring.The letter accused Palm Beach County of never imposing those requirements on another property owner in the county's history.The project's potential noise and other impacts have been closely watched by people living near the proposed data center."It was shocking to say the very least," Arden resident Janice Ridenour said of the letter.Ridenour lives near the data center property and has been outspoken about Project Tango since it was announced.She helped spearhead the western communities' fight against the earlier Project Tango expansion that commissioners rejected in July.After that vote, Ridenour believed residents' efforts had made a difference.The subsequent administrative approval in October left her questioning what those efforts accomplished."We spent a lot of money, you know, on lawyers, and we did our part, you know, and it was for nothing, and here we are again," Ridenour said.Beyond Project Tango itself, both Ridenour and Waldron say they're concerned about what the October approval could mean for other properties across Palm Beach County.They fear it could establish a path for warehouse properties zoned light industrial to be administratively approved for data center uses without a vote by the Palm Beach County Commission.That concern makes the dispute about more than one proposed data center or one neighborhood.For Waldron, the letter also creates a separate question: whether the circumstances surrounding the October decision justify reconsidering it.WPTV will continue following whether Palm Beach County takes steps to nullify or otherwise reconsider the October approval.Hoffman previously reached out to the developers behind Project Tango regarding the October expansion but did not receive a response.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers asked the Vero Beach City Council on Tuesday to take another look at merging emergency dispatch. He pitched it as a way to save money as the city prepares for revenue losses under Amendment 3 . Flowers said he first brought the idea to the council about two years ago. He said Brevard County has since moved to a unified dispatch system, and he told council members his offer still stands. "I'm not asking for anything specific today. I just want to make sure that it's known that it is my desire that we go to a unified dispatch system," Flowers said. He asked that it be considered "as a potential cost savings" as the city makes what he called "difficult decisions" under Amendment 3. Florida voters approved a ballot initiative that will slash non-school property taxes despite a campaign by local officials warning it would gut funding for public safety and other services. It will increase the homestead exemption from about $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Council member Tracey Zudans asked city staff to put numbers on the idea. "I'd love to see some numbers attached to it, not just response time numbers, but also some dollar numbers so that we can share that with our taxpayers as well," Zudans said. "I'd be happy to have my staff work with you guys," Flowers said. Mayor Aaron Vos said city staff will total what the city spends on dispatch now, and Flowers will bring back what it would cost the city to join a countywide call center. Vos said he expects a unified center would be run by the county, not the sheriff, similar to St. Lucie County's. Vice Mayor John Cotugno asked whether the dispatch center would be a county function or run by the sheriff's office. Flowers said the county technically runs dispatch, but most dispatchers work for his agency. "I have the bulk of dispatchers that work for me at the sheriff's office, so I can only offer it from my side," Flowers said. "You would have to ask the county if they were interested in maybe doing it differently." He added that the sheriff's office and the county are still discussing how Amendment 3 will affect their relationship. See also: 22-year-old West Palm Beach motorcyclist struck, killed by SUV in Loxahatchee That relationship has been strained before. In July 2025 a budget debate erupted during an Indian River County Commission meeting, prompting the board to call a 15-minute recess after tensions flared between commissioners and Flowers. Flowers was requesting $93.5 million that year, while the county recommended a budget closer to $83.5 million. Commissioners ultimately voted to raise the sheriff's budget by $6.8 million, far less than he requested. Flowers later sued the commission , which then held a special meeting over the sheriff's budget. "This is a very deep issue," Flowers said. "If we do it as a county, if we do it under me, either way, I'm just trying to get all of our dispatchers in the same room together." Council members took no action on the proposal. Vos said Amendment 3 means the city has to consider every option. "With the implications of Amendment 3, we have to look at all aspects of where we can save money," Vos said. "If it saves us money, that's what we need to do." But Vos said moving dispatch out of the police department could come with a hidden cost. "You could lose some of that rapport between the call center staff and the officers due to familiarity," he said. Vos said he talked with police leaders in Sebastian and Fellsmere after Flowers first pitched the idea. He said Sebastian police used the sheriff's call center until 2007, then went back to running their own. Vero Beach Police Chief David Currey said his position on keeping the city's dispatch center has not changed. Vero Beach and Sebastian police are the only agencies in the county that run their own dispatch. "The dispatchers know the officers. They know the community members," Currey said. "If we don't have that under our umbrella, then I don't have control over any of that." Currey said the department switched to a new computer-aided dispatch and records management system in June. He said the department is working with the sheriff's office to connect the two agencies' dispatch systems, which would let dispatchers see where deputies and officers are and handle calls without transferring them. Currey said the idea last came up around 2012. He said the sheriff at the time told the city that dispatching for Vero Beach would likely cost about the same, if not more. "We have ten dispatchers, and they have salaries, and they have benefits," Currey said. "That will cost him just like it'll cost us." Despite the uncertainty around Amendment 3, Currey said the department is not freezing hiring and is interviewing for a police officer position now.

Four people from Jacksonville, including a 16-year-old, are in custody after the Martin County Sheriff's Office says a 17-year-old heard a suspicious noise outside his family's home in Palm City's Evergreen Club, prompting a 911 call and an extensive overnight search. Investigators say the group parked a vehicle near the C-23 Canal before walking into the gated community and targeting a home. Deputies later recovered masks, gloves and a stolen firearm during their investigation.WATCH: Teen's Alert Leads to 4 Arrests After Palm City ManhuntThe sheriff's office is now asking residents in the Evergreen Club community to check their homes, vehicles and security cameras for anything suspicious as investigators try to determine why the group traveled from Jacksonville to Martin County and whether any other properties were targeted.Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the incident began just after 3 a.m., when the family's 17-year-old son realized something was wrong."The 17-year-old son heard a noise, woke up, knew something was wrong, but didn't quite know what it was," Budensiek said. "(He) went and talked to his parents."The family then began reviewing footage from security cameras around the property.According to Budensiek, one camera was no longer working properly. When the family went farther back through the recorded footage, he said they discovered people moving around the home."They could see that one of their cameras wasn't working," Budensiek said. "They kept going further back in their search history, and saw where these three black males actually were circling the house."Budensiek said the video showed someone placing a sticker over a camera lens near the back door so activity there could no longer be seen.The family called 911.Deputies began searching the area outside the gated community and checked a parking lot near the C-23 Canal."There indeed was a car parked there," Budensiek said.The sheriff's office said the suspects had parked along the canal before walking into the neighborhood.One person was taken into custody near the vehicle, while the others fled, according to the sheriff.Deputies established a perimeter and searched with assistance from aviation and K-9 units and the Stuart Police Department. Budensiek said two of the people who fled were ultimately discovered hiding beneath the bridge carrying Murphy Road over the C-23 Canal."Two fled and ended up hiding under the bridge that crosses the C-23 Canal on Murphy Road," Budensiek said. "They were the last two to actually be apprehended after an extensive manhunt."The three adults arrested were identified as 21-year-old Nathaniel Phillip Wise Jr., 21-year-old Za'kyri Isreal Emmanuel Crews and 21-year-old Cameron Elijah Mapson. A 16-year-old was also arrested, but WPTV is not identifying the juvenile.All four face attempted home invasion charges, according to published reports citing the sheriff's office. Wise also faces grand theft of a firearm and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon. As investigators retraced the route between the suspects' vehicle and the family's home, Budensiek said they recovered a handgun."They recovered a handgun that was stolen with an extended magazine, and were able to corroborate again what the intended victim said," Budensiek said.The Sheriff's Office has also reported recovering masks and gloves during the investigation. Investigators are now trying to determine why this particular home may have been targeted."We don't know why that house," Budensiek said. "We don't know if they went to any other houses potentially in the middle of the night."The sheriff's office is asking residents to review their security footage and inspect their homes and vehicles for missing property or possible evidence of another attempted break-in.Anyone who discovers missing property or signs of a break-in is asked to contact the Martin County Sheriff's Office at 772-220-7060.Investigators are also examining digital evidence as they work to establish why the four made the trip from Jacksonville to Palm City.MORE PALM CITY: Judge rejects motion to dismiss animal cruelty case against Palm City dog trainer Nikki CamerlengoThis story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

For some children, the biggest worry this holiday season should be who gets caught first in a game of hide-and-seek or who can throw a football the farthest.But for families facing housing insecurity, the reality can be much different.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE HERE: For more than four decades, Adopt-A-Family of the Palm Beaches has worked to make sure families with children have a safe, stable place to call home.The nonprofit provides affordable and supportive housing for families experiencing homelessness or at risk of losing their homes. Its work also extends beyond housing, offering resources designed to help parents and children build long-term stability.At one of the organization's residential campuses, families live within walking distance of a playground, where children have a place to play while their parents work toward a more secure future."We are surrounded by 87 units of supportive housing which are located within a tenth of a mile of this playground," said Matt Constantine, CEO of Adopt-A-Family of the Palm Beaches.Constantine says the campus setting allows the organization to bring several services directly to the families it serves.Those resources include educational support for children, after-school programming, career coaching, case management and on-site mental health services.The goal is to address the challenges that can make it difficult for families to remain housed and financially independent."Provide housing stability to families with children who are either experiencing homelessness or at risk of becoming homeless," Constantine said, describing the organization's longstanding mission.But as housing costs continue to rise, the need for assistance is growing."Our phones ring all day long," Constantine said.He says the upfront cost of securing a rental property can be a significant obstacle for families already struggling financially."And the first, last, and security deposit comes out to almost eight thousand dollars, ten thousand dollars," he said.Children are also at the center of the organization's work. Constantine says roughly two-thirds of the people served by Adopt-A-Family are children, making educational and emotional support an important part of its mission."Two-thirds of who we serve are children, so a big responsibility that we have and a big component of the work we do is to be there for that next generation," Constantine said.Through United Way of Palm Beach County's Season of Hope campaign, Adopt-A-Family is among the local nonprofit agencies receiving community support to continue its work helping families in need.For Constantine, the effort is about more than providing assistance during the holidays. It's about neighbors stepping up for one another."I think that's the secret of building a healthy community. It's being there for your neighbor," he said.HOW TO HELP:Community members interested in supporting Adopt-A-Family of the Palm Beaches can learn more about its programs, make a donation or explore volunteer opportunities by visiting www.aafpbc.org.

People across South Florida and the Treasure Coast are bracing for yet another round of heavy rain, and one Indian River County community is pleading for help after battling repeated flooding this month.Joe Waters documented his frustration Saturday evening, recording on his phone in front of his mobile home in the Heritage Plantation mobile home park near Vero Beach as a car drove through floodwaters that almost covered its headlights.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Waters said the wake caused by passing vehicles crashed into the bricks that protect the undercarriage of his home, toppling them."The water came up probably about thigh high," Waters said. "Came up into the driveway, went into the house."Waters and his wife were able to clean their home, but he said his car is still in the shop with $4,600 worth of damage, waiting on approval from the insurance company.When we showed up at Heritage Plantation Tuesday afternoon, a crowd of neighbors gathered — fed up after battling multiple floods just this month.Dawn Carboni, the HOA president, told me she wants to be a voice for her neighbors, especially those who can't speak up."They just want to feel safe in their homes," she said.The flooding has created dangerous conditions for emergency responders, Carboni said."We had a gentleman who needed EMS to come out, and they could not get to his home, so they had to park out on 82nd (Avenue), and then a large fire truck had to get to the home," Carboni said.With more heavy rain in the forecast, Carboni said residents are frightened."People are afraid. It's horrible living in fear when you don't know if it's going to rain and you're going to be able to leave your home the next day."She wants to spread awareness about what her community is going through."We need help, and we're asking for help," Carboni said.Emergency managers in Indian River County tell me they're operating at a Level 2 emergency, meaning the Emergency Operations Center is partially activated. They've extended the state of emergency through Sunday, Nov. 30.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Home Business News and Economic Updates in Sebastian, Florida Sheriff renews call for unified 911 dispatch as Vero Beach faces Amendment 3 cuts by Tina Hodges Nov 25, 2026 / 9:35 AM A A A A Reset Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers (City of Vero Beach) Share on Twitter Share via Email VERO BEACH— Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers stood before the Vero Beach City Council on Tuesday and asked council members to reconsider combining the city’s emergency dispatch with the sheriff’s office. He said unifying dispatch across the county has been one of his goals since taking office. “One of my goals since being elected sheriff was to unify public safety dispatch for our entire county under one roof,” Flowers told Sebastian Daily . “St. Lucie and others have had this for decades, and it just makes sense from a safety standpoint, communications perspective, and an overall reduction of duplicative services. It’s my hope that with Amendment 3 passing, as cities look to find ways to reduce costs, a unified public safety dispatch system will be one of the first choices.” He originally raised the idea with the council about two years ago. Since then, Brevard County has moved to a single dispatch center. Flowers hopes the city will consider the concept as it works through what he called “difficult decisions” under the amendment. Voters approved Amendment 3 earlier this month to raise the homestead exemption on non-school property taxes from roughly $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and to $250,000 in 2028. Local officials had opposed the measure, warning it would cut into funding for public safety and other services. Council member Tracey Zudans asked for concrete numbers. “I’d love to see some numbers attached to it, not just response time numbers, but also some dollar numbers so that we can share that with our taxpayers as well,” she said. Flowers said his staff would work with the city on the figures. Mayor Aaron Vos said staff will first calculate what the city currently spends on dispatch, and Flowers will come back with an estimate of what it would cost the city to join a countywide center. Vos said he expects the county, not the sheriff’s office, would run any unified operation — the same arrangement used in St. Lucie County. Vice Mayor John Cotugno asked whether the center would be a county function or under the sheriff. Flowers said the county technically oversees dispatch, though most of the dispatchers work for his agency. “I have the bulk of dispatchers that work for me at the sheriff’s office, so I can only offer it from my side,” he said. “You would have to ask the county if they were interested in maybe doing it differently.” Council members took no formal action on the proposal. Four people from Jacksonville, including a 16-year-old, are in custody after the Martin County Sheriff's Office says a 17-year-old heard a suspicious noise outside his family's home in Palm City's Evergreen Club, prompting a 911 call and an extensive overnight search. Investigators say the group parked a vehicle near the C-23 Canal before walking into the gated community and targeting a home. Deputies later recovered masks, gloves and a stolen firearm during their investigation.WATCH: Teen's Alert Leads to 4 Arrests After Palm City ManhuntThe sheriff's office is now asking residents in the Evergreen Club community to check their homes, vehicles and security cameras for anything suspicious as investigators try to determine why the group traveled from Jacksonville to Martin County and whether any other properties were targeted.Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the incident began just after 3 a.m., when the family's 17-year-old son realized something was wrong."The 17-year-old son heard a noise, woke up, knew something was wrong, but didn't quite know what it was," Budensiek said. "(He) went and talked to his parents."The family then began reviewing footage from security cameras around the property.According to Budensiek, one camera was no longer working properly. When the family went farther back through the recorded footage, he said they discovered people moving around the home."They could see that one of their cameras wasn't working," Budensiek said. "They kept going further back in their search history, and saw where these three black males actually were circling the house."Budensiek said the video showed someone placing a sticker over a camera lens near the back door so activity there could no longer be seen.The family called 911.Deputies began searching the area outside the gated community and checked a parking lot near the C-23 Canal."There indeed was a car parked there," Budensiek said.The sheriff's office said the suspects had parked along the canal before walking into the neighborhood.One person was taken into custody near the vehicle, while the others fled, according to the sheriff.Deputies established a perimeter and searched with assistance from aviation and K-9 units and the Stuart Police Department. Budensiek said two of the people who fled were ultimately discovered hiding beneath the bridge carrying Murphy Road over the C-23 Canal."Two fled and ended up hiding under the bridge that crosses the C-23 Canal on Murphy Road," Budensiek said. "They were the last two to actually be apprehended after an extensive manhunt."The three adults arrested were identified as 21-year-old Nathaniel Phillip Wise Jr., 21-year-old Za'kyri Isreal Emmanuel Crews and 21-year-old Cameron Elijah Mapson. A 16-year-old was also arrested, but WPTV is not identifying the juvenile.All four face attempted home invasion charges, according to published reports citing the sheriff's office. Wise also faces grand theft of a firearm and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon. As investigators retraced the route between the suspects' vehicle and the family's home, Budensiek said they recovered a handgun."They recovered a handgun that was stolen with an extended magazine, and were able to corroborate again what the intended victim said," Budensiek said.The Sheriff's Office has also reported recovering masks and gloves during the investigation. Investigators are now trying to determine why this particular home may have been targeted."We don't know why that house," Budensiek said. "We don't know if they went to any other houses potentially in the middle of the night."The sheriff's office is asking residents to review their security footage and inspect their homes and vehicles for missing property or possible evidence of another attempted break-in.Anyone who discovers missing property or signs of a break-in is asked to contact the Martin County Sheriff's Office at 772-220-7060.Investigators are also examining digital evidence as they work to establish why the four made the trip from Jacksonville to Palm City.MORE PALM CITY: Judge rejects motion to dismiss animal cruelty case against Palm City dog trainer Nikki CamerlengoThis story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A Port St. Lucie family is remembering their 24-year-old daughter after she was killed in a hit-and-run last week. Alexis Cuellar, known to her family as Lexi, was riding her scooter to work on Nov. 16 when she was struck by a vehicle near SW Gatlin Boulevard, according to police. She died the following day, Nov. 17. For the first time, her father and relatives are sharing memories of the young woman they say brought joy to everyone around her. Alexis wasn't just a ray of sunshine, you know. I think to us she was just the sun, her father, Alberto Vasquez, said As the eldest daughter, Vasquez said Alexis had a natural instinct to care for others, beginning with her own siblings. Ever since she was born she just, she had a passion for caring for others, starting with her siblings, you know, he said. At the family's Port St. Lucie home, Vasquez and relatives, some visiting from Texas, gathered around photos of Alexis as they remembered her life. She was the sweetest person ever, and it's a huge loss for the family, her aunt, Minerva Benitez, said. Also read: Port St. Lucie hit-and-run victim dies; driver could face more serious charges Vasquez said the support they have received has helped them. It's really helped us get through these first difficult days that were unbearable, he said. He remembered his daughter as someone who loved children and dreamed of working with them. He was also proud of her time in Junior ROTC. On the morning of the crash, Vasquez watched Alexis leave home for her job at Wendy's. She had been excited about picking up more hours. He said he saw her riding away on her scooter and assumed she would be OK. Five minutes later, he learned there had been a crash. Police have charged 18-year-old Tristian Ray Sanchez-Chasmer in connection with the crash. Investigators say he had been playing ding-dong-ditch with friends before getting behind the wheel of a Chevy Tahoe. He's accused of hitting Cuellar as she rode her scooter in a crosswalk, then leaving the scene. He is currently charged with leaving the scene. Additional charges, including vehicular homicide, could follow. Vasquez said he wishes he could have been there to help his daughter. I'm sorry that I couldn't be there for her, maybe help her. And that I loved her deeply because I didn't get a chance to tell her that, he said. Now, he is preparing a place at home where he plans to bring her. A service for Alexis will be held Wednesday, Nov. 25, at Haisley Funeral Home in Fort Pierce. Police are continuing to investigate the crash.

A Palm City teenager's quick thinking may have stopped four men from breaking into his family's home at the Evergreen Club community off Murphy Road. The Martin County Sheriff's Office says the 17-year-old boy heard a noise outside their home on SW Bimini Circle at 3 a.m. Tuesday. He alerted his parents who called 911, interrupting the home invasion. When deputies arrived at the scene, the four suspects, three men and a teenager from Jacksonville, ran away in different directions. The sheriff's office says deputies set up a perimeter around the neighborhood with help from its aviation team, K-9 unit, and the Stuart Police Department. K9's were able to track down all four suspects hiding in separate locations throughout the community. The teen was found hiding in a bush outside the community. Two of the men were found hiding under a nearby bridge off Murphy Road. The fourth person was in a nearby parking lot who detectives believe was the getaway driver. The sheriff's office says at least one of the suspects was armed with a handgun. Sheriff John Budensiek said three of the four suspects have violent criminal histories. "These are bad, bad individuals who drove at least three and a half hours to Martin County to victimize a family that was going throughout their normal nightly routines," Budensiek said. Investigators said the suspects parked along the canal and walked half a mile into the neighborhood to target the home. The group is seen on home security video around 3 a.m. wearing dark clothing, masks and gloves. The sheriff said they tried to break in through a back door and covered a surveillance camera lens with a sticker. Deputies found masks, gloves and a firearm that had been stolen. Homeowners at the Evergreen Club community were shaken up. "I immediately woke up to Facebook and texts this morning, friends and family asked me if I was okay," said resident Katherine Willis. "Absolutely shocked that they would try to come in here. What are you going to get out of here? It's just very out of the ordinary for sure." The suspects were identified as: Nathaniel Phillip Wise Jr, 22 Za'kyri Isreal Emmanuel Crews, 21 Cameron Elijah Mapson, 21 Teenage boy, 16 All four were charged with attempted home invasion. Wise faces an additional charge of grand theft and possession of a firearm. They're all being held in the Martin County Jail without bond. See also: Boca Raton police arrest man after reported assault on El Rio Trail The agency is asking Palm City residents to check their homes and vehicles for missing property or signs of a break-in. Anyone who finds anything missing should call the sheriff’s office at 772-220-7060. "The Martin County Sheriff's Office is heavily invested in protecting our community," Budensiek said. "To these traveling criminals, we're gonna put you away forever if we can."

Thanksgiving came with a little extra help for families in Delray Beach as local high school students teamed up with police officers to make sure they had a holiday meal on the table.Students from Atlantic High School’s Criminal Justice Academy partnered with the Delray Beach Police Department to deliver more than a dozen full Thanksgiving meals to families in need across the city.WATCH: Atlantic High School students, Delray Beach police deliver Thanksgiving meals to families in needFor the students, the annual effort is about more than dropping off food. It’s an opportunity to learn what it means to serve the community beyond the classroom.“It teaches you to be less selfish and care more about what is going on around you and how you can help,” student Alexis Felicetta said.The students went door to door alongside Delray Beach police officers, personally delivering the meals and meeting the families receiving them.“We are helping families, and seeing them smile when they open the door makes me happy,” student Micaja Paul Joseph said.The Thanksgiving meal giveaway has become a tradition for the Criminal Justice Academy and Delray Beach police, continuing for more than decade.Major Gary Ferreri with the Delray Beach Police Department said the experience also gives students perspective on hardships other people in their community may be facing.“Some of the kids come from tough situations. They get to see that even as bad as they have it, there are others that have it tougher sometimes.”For one family, the delivery meant being able to have a Thanksgiving turkey without worrying about how to pay for it.“We didn't really have money to buy a turkey for Thanksgiving,” a family member said. “For me, it's happy because I get to spend more time with my family.”For the students, police officers and families taking part, the tradition is proving a little help can go a long way.

The Florida Panthers held practice at Baptist Health Iceplex in Fort Lauderdale Tuesday morning.Anticipation is building for the Wednesday night matchup against the Ottawa Senators at Amerant Bank Arena.Watch report from Mike Trim:Perhaps the largest source of that anticipation is the potential return of two Panther superstars: Captain Aleksander Barkov and Brad Marchand.While not confirming the two stars would be inserted back into the lineup Wednesday, head coach Paul Maurice addressed the media after practice and said, “There's a possibility it's both.”After missing all of last season to a right knee injury, Barkov returned to the Panthers lineup this season only to injure his left knee in the second game.Marchand was injured the following game.Neither has played since their injuries.Speaking about Barkov, Maurice said, “I mean, he's one of the best players in the world, and we just haven't had him here for a year and a half. Big trades around the league. I think we made the biggest one. We got Barkov for nothing.”Panthers defenseman Niko Mikkola talked about the boost Barkov would give the team.“Oh, it's huge. He's the face of the team, leader, and our most important player, so it's, it's huge.”This will be Panthers forward Brady Tkachuk’s first time facing his old team here in Florida.Tkachuk played eight seasons in Ottawa, serving as captain the last five.WPTV Florida Panthers anchor Mike Trim connected with Tkachuk after practice with other members of the media.“This new chapter has been awesome and to have this game at home, it's still going to be different, but I'm really excited about doing it in front of our home fans.”A special promotion for Wednesday night’s game will have a Thanksgiving theme.The first 10,000 fans into the arena will receive a Panthers oven mitt.Puck drop is set for 7 p.m. Wednesday.The game will be shown on WPTV and The Spot South Florida.

The Miami Dolphins were on the practice field Wednesday as they prepare for Sunday's battle against the New York Jets. The rain forced the team indoors, but that didn't stop the Fins from bringing nonstop energy at practice.WATCH REPORT BELOW: On the injury front, cornerback Juju Brents was out Wednesday, but everyone else was a full go.Although the rain tore through South Florida on Thanksgiving Eve, the Dolphins laced up their cleats to prepare for the New York Jets."This is going to be a long season, and there is always going to be a Thanksgiving, there is always going to be a Thanksgiving, a Christmas, and other holidays, and you have to push through," head coach Jeff Hafley said.Rain stormed through South Florida this week, but it didn't slow the grind for new quarterback Kyle McCord, who's learning the NFL game on the fly as he and the Fins welcome the Jets to Hard Rock Stadium this Sunday.In Week 7, the Dolphins beat the Jets 28-25 at MetLife Stadium to earn their only win of the season."It's just another great opportunity to keep growing and keep rolling and keep getting better," McCord said. With two starts under his belt, McCord credits rookie wide receiver Caleb Douglas with helping ease him into a new role."There's a reason we try to get him the ball; he's a great player, but at the same time we're both young players in the league and continuing to grow," McCord said.For Douglas, he's shown the most promise on offense, but like any rookie, he's had some growing pains, including drops.So Wednesday afternoon, he worked with specialized glasses to help with vision, but number seven has his eyes set on Sunday's game against their division rival."I'm really excited and blessed with another opportunity to go out there and keep proving it," said Douglas.With Thanksgiving on Thursday, we wanted to know what these guys have on their plates."I'm getting a little bit of everything, you know. I'm getting some Turkey, some ham, mac and cheese, some collard greens," offensive lineman Austin Jackson said."I hope I go home today and Ma Duke's got the kitchen good, man. I can't wait to get that first scoop of macaroni and greens," running back Ollie Gordon said.

A new holiday tradition is taking root at the Jupiter Inlet Lighthouse, where Luminary Nights will bring holiday lights, nighttime lighthouse climbs, local music and shopping to the historic waterfront property in December.The limited event is scheduled for Dec. 11, 12, 18, and 19. Organizers say they are starting small this year with hopes of growing Luminary Nights into an annual family tradition in northern Palm Beach County."We really hope to make this a new family-friendly holiday tradition here in North County," Executive Director Katrina Heller said.A Banyan tree (ficus) that dances to musicOne of the most visual additions will be the Lighthouse's illuminated Banyan tree.Organizers have nicknamed it the "Dancing Tree" because its lights have been synchronized to music."We have lit it up and timed it to music, so we're calling it our dancing tree, and we'll have a new program every half hour," Heller said.Luminary Nights will also feature nighttime lighthouse climbs, holiday shopping, live music and a Kids Zone for families.Lighthouse climbs are limited and available on a first-come, first-served basis. Children must be at least 48 inches tall to climb.Tickets are $30 for adults and $20 for children. A family ticket for two adults and two children is $75.Keeping the holiday celebration localEvent Manager Simone Incendy said organizers are intentionally incorporating local businesses and musicians into Luminary Nights.The Vendor Village will feature local artists and small businesses, including vendors whose products are carried in the Lighthouse gift shop.Incendy said area high school bands and community bands will also be among the performers.The approach connects the new celebration to the community surrounding the landmark while giving small businesses and local performers another place to reach visitors during the holiday season.Proceeds from the event will go toward preserving the Jupiter Inlet Lighthouse, its history and its educational programming, according to event information provided by organizers.A new view of the Jupiter Inlet LighthouseThe holiday celebration isn't the only new attraction visitors will find at the Lighthouse.Heller said a shoreline restoration project is wrapping up with a grand opening scheduled for Dec. 3 at 1 p.m.The work includes a new seawall and a boardwalk stretching more than 800 feet around the point where the Loxahatchee River and Indian River meet."We're so excited for our new boardwalk," Heller said.She said the boardwalk will give visitors a new perspective of the Lighthouse property and the surrounding water, including opportunities to see fish below.For a landmark built around a light that has guided the Jupiter waterfront for generations, the additions bring together its past and future: a restored shoreline and new waterfront experience alongside a holiday celebration organizers hope families will return to year after year.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Hundreds of Palm Beach County families are getting help putting Thanksgiving dinner on the table through SPECTRA, the nonprofit arm of the Palm Beach County Housing Authority, as community partners work to address food insecurity during the holiday season.SPECTRA recently helped distribute 300 frozen turkeys and is now preparing Thanksgiving fixings for families in South Bay, according to Naderge Alcime, ROSS coordinator with the Palm Beach County Housing Authority.WATCH REPORT BELOW:The assistance comes as the Housing Authority says more than 280 additional families are on its waiting list for help.Filling needs beyond housingSPECTRA was created to help address needs that extend beyond putting a roof over someone's head."SPECTRA is our not-for-profit arm of the Housing Authority," Chief Financial Officer Tad Fuller said. "The Housing Authority, of course, houses individuals and families within our county. The 19-year-old son of a Florida county commissioner was shot and killed while camping in Santa Rosa County on Sunday.Carey Washington Vinson, a history major at Florida State University, was the son of Joe Vinson, who was recently elected to the Escambia County Commission.The Santa Rosa County Sheriff's Office said investigators are working to identify those involved in Carey's death and determine the circumstances surrounding the shooting. No arrests have been announced.In an emotional Facebook post Tuesday, Joe Vinson remembered his son, whom the family affectionately called "Wash," and pushed back against suggestions that his death was an accident."This was not a freak hunting accident — not someone firing carelessly in the dark," Vinson wrote. "It was not a 'stray bullet' that killed our Wash."According to Vinson, the family understands that someone stood on the opposite bank of the river and pointed a gun toward the occupied sandbar campground.He said the shooters were close enough to see the campfire and hear people talking."They fired shot after shot with malicious intent," Vinson wrote, alleging that the shooters fired another round after campers screamed for them to stop, then laughed as they drove away.Those details reflect the family's understanding of the shooting. The sheriff's office has not publicly confirmed that account in the statement provided.Vinson remembered his son as a thoughtful, outgoing young man who loved history, music and adventure. Carey was an excellent debater, played piano and guitar, and had recently been accepted into a summer study-abroad program in Valencia."Most of all, he had a tender and loving heart — for his friends and family, for his girlfriend, for animals, for the marginalized," Vinson wrote. "He was quick to laugh and easy to love.""I can't believe I'll never feel his hugs again, or hear him bickering with his siblings," his father wrote. "I can't believe any of this."The Santa Rosa County Sheriff's Office is asking anyone who witnessed suspicious activity near Deaton Bridge Road and Boat Ramp Road, or who has information that could help identify those involved, to contact investigators.Anyone with information can call the sheriff's office at 850-983-1190, Option 1.Anonymous tips can also be submitted to Santa Rosa Crime Stoppers at 850-437-STOP (7867) or through the P3 Tips mobile app."I know it won't bring back Wash, but I would sleep better knowing they can't hurt anyone else," Vinson wrote.

King tides are the highest tides of the year, and they are increasingly flooding coastal communities as sea levels rise.King tide is a non-scientific or colloquial term that people often use to describe these exceptionally high tides. The 2026 super El Niño — the natural and temporary warming of parts of the Pacific — has raised coastal water levels and intensified the effects of king tides."Tides are incredibly complicated. Really every location has different tidal cycles and that's the basis for what a king tide is," said Alec Bogdanoff, an oceanographer and meteorologist in Fort Lauderdale, Florida. "It's a local term for the highest high tides of the year in a location. And when it impacts you, that's when they call it a king tide."King tides are happening more oftenKing tides typically occur when the sun, moon and Earth are nearly aligned because their gravitational pull adds together. This raises water levels and produces the greatest tidal effects of the year. This can happen on both coasts around the same time because the tides are responding to the same alignment and proximity of the moon and sun. In 2026, El Niño caused higher baseline water levels on both coasts, Bogdanoff said.The highest high tides happen during full moons and new moons and seasonal cycles that can raise or lower sea levels, he added.Historically, many coastal areas saw king tides once or twice a year, but some places are experiencing them more often than that as sea levels rise.King tides can cause floods in coastal communitiesBecause king tides bring unusually high water levels, they can cause local tidal flooding. Strong winds and storms can make that flooding worse.Bogdanoff said the stormwater systems don't function normally when ocean water is higher than the levels they were designed for.Climate change is raising risksClimate change is driving and accelerating sea level rise. Glaciers and ice sheets are melting and the sea's waters are expanding as they warm. As this happens, flooding from king tides is becoming more frequent and it's increasingly disrupting life along the coasts.Four California locations recorded their all-time highest observed water levels in late October, and near-record king tides flooded some low-lying communities there as Thanksgiving travel ramped up."El Niño is natural, the sea level rise we're seeing now isn't," Bogdanoff said. "The flooding we're seeing with these king tides is a preview of what's to come in the 2030s and beyond."In 2011, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency said sea level rise will make current king tides become the future's everyday tides.Coastal areas prepare for king tidesBogdanoff said coastal communities can do stormwater assessments and adaptation plans that take into account future projections for sea level rise, like his home state is doing with its Resilient Florida Program. Bogdanoff is principal scientist and co-founder of Brizaga, an engineering and consulting firm that helps communities plan for flooding and sea level rise.Next steps could include raising roads, figuring out better ways to protect the coastlines, finding more green space that absorbs water and building bigger stormwater systems that rely more on pumps than gravity to drain the water quicker — projects that will take time, he added."In some communities it's a much bigger conversation about what the future looks like," he said. "We don't have to fix everything at once. We just need to make sure the next decision is a little smarter than the last one."

Federal disaster aid is now available for residents in Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast affected by recent flooding.FEMA announced late Tuesday that federal disaster assistance is available to individuals and families in Indian River, Martin, Okeechobee, Palm Beach, St. Lucie and Brevard counties as recovery efforts continue.U.S. Rep. Lois Frankel said in a statement the declaration unlocks critical federal recovery resources for residents, businesses and local governments devastated by the flooding.The assistance can include grants for temporary housing and home repairs, low-cost loans to cover uninsured property losses and other programs designed to help people recover from the disaster.Residents who suffered damage or other losses should first file a claim with their insurance provider. They can then apply for FEMA assistance through DisasterAssistance.gov, by calling 1-800-621-3362 or through the FEMA App.Those who use a relay service, including video relay or captioned telephone services, should provide FEMA with the number for that service when applying.Federal funding is also available on a cost-sharing basis to state, tribal and eligible local governments, as well as certain private nonprofit organizations, for debris removal and emergency protective measures. That assistance is available in Palm Beach, Martin, Indian River, Okeechobee, Brevard and Hardee, counties.Frankel said that Palm Beach County officials estimate that $53 million in disaster assistance is needed countywide — nearly $35 million to help individuals and families recover and more than $18 million to help local governments cover emergency response and cleanup costs.Additional counties could be designated for federal assistance later, depending on the results of continuing damage assessments.What residents should do:File a claim with their insurance provider.Apply for federal assistance at DisasterAssistance.gov, through the FEMA App or by calling 1-800-621-3362.Severe storms and flooding have impacted parts of Florida since Oct. 31, prompting the state to ask for the federal disaster declaration.

The City of Stuart is warning local businesses and contractors about a fraudulent email scam involving fake invoices for development, building, planning, or project-related fees. According to the City, several businesses with active projects and applications have recently reported receiving emails claiming to be from the City of Stuart and requesting thousands of dollars in fees. In some cases recipients were instructed to wire funds. The City says it does not send invoices by email for these purposes, and that all official City development and permitting fees must be paid through the City’s official OpenGov application portal. One of the fraudulent email addresses reported to the City is: commissions.stuartfl.gov@usa.com. The City encourages applicants with active projects to remain vigilant and carefully review all correspondence related to their projects to prevent getting scammed.

A Palm City teenager's quick thinking may have stopped four men from breaking into his family's home at the Evergreen Club community off Murphy Road. The Martin County Sheriff's Office says the 17-year-old boy heard a noise outside their home on SW Bimini Circle at 3 a.m. Tuesday. He alerted his parents who called 911, interrupting the home invasion. When deputies arrived at the scene, the four suspects, three men and a teenager from Jacksonville, ran away in different directions. The sheriff's office says deputies set up a perimeter around the neighborhood with help from its aviation team, K-9 unit, and the Stuart Police Department. K9's were able to track down all four suspects hiding in separate locations throughout the community. The teen was found hiding in a bush outside the community. Two of the men were found hiding under a nearby bridge off Murphy Road. The fourth person was in a nearby parking lot who detectives believe was the getaway driver. The sheriff's office says at least one of the suspects was armed with a handgun. Sheriff John Budensiek said three of the four suspects have violent criminal histories. "These are bad, bad individuals who drove at least three and a half hours to Martin County to victimize a family that was going throughout their normal nightly routines," Budensiek said. Investigators said the suspects parked along the canal and walked half a mile into the neighborhood to target the home. The group is seen on home security video around 3 a.m. wearing dark clothing, masks and gloves. The sheriff said they tried to break in through a back door and covered a surveillance camera lens with a sticker. Deputies found masks, gloves and a firearm that had been stolen. Homeowners at the Evergreen Club community were shaken up. "I immediately woke up to Facebook and texts this morning, friends and family asked me if I was okay," said resident Katherine Willis. "Absolutely shocked that they would try to come in here. What are you going to get out of here? It's just very out of the ordinary for sure." The suspects were identified as: Nathaniel Phillip Wise Jr, 22 Za'kyri Isreal Emmanuel Crews, 21 Cameron Elijah Mapson, 21 Teenage boy, 16 All four were charged with attempted home invasion. Wise faces an additional charge of grand theft and possession of a firearm. They're all being held in the Martin County Jail without bond. See also: Boca Raton police arrest man after reported assault on El Rio Trail The agency is asking Palm City residents to check their homes and vehicles for missing property or signs of a break-in. Anyone who finds anything missing should call the sheriff’s office at 772-220-7060. "The Martin County Sheriff's Office is heavily invested in protecting our community," Budensiek said. "To these traveling criminals, we're gonna put you away forever if we can."

A Palm City family was shaken early Tuesday morning when three masked men, at least one armed, attempted to break into their home on Bimini Circle. The homeowner asked WPBF 25 News to not use their names but said his 17-year-old son was the first to hear the suspects as they tried to get in around 3 a.m. In an exclusive statement, the homeowner said, "My son heard them trying to jiggle open all three of our patio sliders fairly aggressively." The son woke his mother and father, and the father armed himself. "I grabbed my AR-15 and proceeded into the house as she called 911," he said. The homeowner believes the suspects got spooked after he turned off the outside lights. "They must have seen me through the windows and seen the lights go out and left," he said. "We're a bit shook from the experience but doing good and feel blessed and lucky." Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said his office deployed every resource they had to find the suspects. "We knew these were bad guys," he said. Authorities launched an extensive search for the suspects, using aerial resources and K-9 units. One suspect was found hiding in bushes outside the community, another near what they believe was the getaway car, and two others were discovered under a nearby bridge. The Sheriff's Office identified the suspects as 21-year-old Nathaniel Phillip Wise Jr., 21-year-old Za'kyri Isreal Emmanuel Crews, and 21-year-old Cameron Elijah Mapson. A fourth suspect is 16 years old. All four suspects are charged with attempted home invasion and are being held at the Martin County jail without bond. The sheriff said the suspects are from Jacksonville, and three of them have extensive criminal records. "These are bad, bad individuals who drove at least three and a half hours to Martin County to victimize a family that was going about their normal nightly routines," Budensiek said. One question investigators are still trying to answer is why the suspects chose this particular home. Budensiek said it's unclear if the attack was random or if the family was targeted. "We don't know the answer to that. We don't know why that house. We don't know if they went to any other houses potentially in the middle of the night," Budensiek said. Authorities are asking residents in the area to check their cameras, cars, and homes for any signs of suspicious activity and to contact the sheriff's office with any information. "Came up into the driveway, went into the house."Waters and his wife were able to clean their home, but he said his car is still in the shop with $4,600 worth of damage, waiting on approval from the insurance company.When we showed up at Heritage Plantation Tuesday afternoon, a crowd of neighbors gathered — fed up after battling multiple floods just this month.Dawn Carboni, the HOA president, told me she wants to be a voice for her neighbors, especially those who can't speak up."They just want to feel safe in their homes," she said.The flooding has created dangerous conditions for emergency responders, Carboni said."We had a gentleman who needed EMS to come out, and they could not get to his home, so they had to park out on 82nd (Avenue), and then a large fire truck had to get to the home," Carboni said.With more heavy rain in the forecast, Carboni said residents are frightened."People are afraid.
